1.title: Mainland Greece
1.hook: At Mycenae a stone gate guards a palace; in Athens, small voting objects open a different question about who could belong.

storyBeats.title: Before the city-state
storyBeats.text: Begin with the Lion Gate, palace remains and tombs at Mycenae. These belong to a Bronze Age world of administration, production and Mediterranean exchange. Read the archaeological evidence alongside the later myths, keeping the two distinct.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Second millennium BCE

storyBeats.title: A city makes its claims
storyBeats.text: The Acropolis gives civic religion a monumental setting. Down in the Agora, building footprints and museum objects bring courts, voting, commerce and daily life into view. The contrast asks how public institutions worked in space, and who was included in their community.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Classical Athens; chiefly fifth-century BCE temples

storyBeats.title: The Greek story keeps moving
storyBeats.text: Epidaurus joins healing, ritual and theatre; Mystras carries the journey into painted Byzantine churches. Greek history extends through Macedonian, Roman, Orthodox and modern worlds. Later Europeans repeatedly reused its forms and ideas, often for purposes quite different from those of their makers.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Classical and Hellenistic sanctuaries; later Byzantine towns

1.takeaway: Compare who organised each place, who used it and how its meaning changed when later societies inherited it.
chapterQuestions: How did Greek communities organise power, worship, exchange, art and knowledge?
What changes when a palace, an agora and a healing sanctuary become your evidence?
1.geographySummary: Athens and Attica connect to Corinth, Nafplio and the Argolid. Delphi or the western Peloponnese is a deliberate extension; northern Greece is another route choice.
1.chronologySummary: Bronze Age palaces → competing Greek cities and shared sanctuaries → Macedonian, Roman and Byzantine layers → modern Greece.

2.title: Rome–Campania
2.hook: From Rome’s ceremonial centre to a Pompeian shop, the scale of the empire changes when you look at the people who kept it running.

storyBeats.title: Power takes up space
storyBeats.text: In the Forum and on the Palatine, temples, council spaces and successive residences show the movement from civic competition toward concentrated imperial authority. The imperial capital supplies one view of Rome; baths, roads and the port at Ostia reveal the infrastructure beneath its display.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Republican and imperial Rome

storyBeats.title: An empire at household scale
storyBeats.text: Around Vesuvius, Pompeii and Herculaneum bring rooms, shops, work and consumption into focus. Paintings, graffiti and surviving objects put ordinary lives beside the capital's monuments. The eruption's human consequences belong to this account alongside the unusual preservation of urban evidence.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Roman towns buried in 79 CE

storyBeats.title: Rome becomes many later Romes
storyBeats.text: San Clemente makes religious and urban change visible through successive underground levels. St Peter's and the Vatican collections show Christian authority and later artistic patronage. Bourbon Caserta joins court ceremony to gardens, water engineering and silk production, continuing the story far beyond antiquity.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Roman and medieval reuse; Renaissance, Baroque and eighteenth-century courts

2.takeaway: Set the imperial capital beside a provincial household, then follow how buildings and objects acquired new religious and political uses.
chapterQuestions: How did Rome sustain an empire and an urban society?
What can a shop, a water system or a reused sacred space add to an imperial monument?
2.geographySummary: Rome and Vatican City form the first base; Naples and its bay form the second. Pompeii and Herculaneum sit within the Naples orbit.
2.chronologySummary: Greek and Etruscan foundations → Republican and imperial Rome → Christian reuse → Renaissance and Baroque patronage → Bourbon and modern layers.

3.title: Istanbul–Marmara
3.hook: A ferry crosses the strait while the city’s monuments cross centuries: Roman institutions, Byzantine sacred art and Ottoman court life remain in conversation.

storyBeats.title: Above and beneath Constantinople
storyBeats.text: Hagia Sophia sets domes, marble, mosaics and later Ottoman additions within one sacred building. Nearby, the Basilica Cistern shifts attention underground to columns, vaults and water storage. Together they let you compare imperial ceremony with the provisioning that made a capital possible.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Sixth-century Constantinople; later sacred reuse

storyBeats.title: The Ottoman city builds institutions
storyBeats.text: At Topkapı, courts and controlled approaches organise government and the imperial household. Mosque complexes connect religious patronage to institutions around them; bazaars and hans bring commerce into the same urban account. Palaces and markets reveal different workings of the city.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Fifteenth–nineteenth-century court; sixteenth–seventeenth-century complexes

storyBeats.title: The strait connects communities
storyBeats.text: Galata, Pera and the Bosphorus carry the story through maritime exchange, minority communities and a later cosmopolitan city. The Jewish museum connects Sephardic migration after 1492 to Ottoman lives. Modern art and an Asian-shore neighbourhood keep this chapter rooted in a city that continues to change.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Sephardic migration after 1492; Ottoman and modern communities

3.takeaway: Read the city across water and across layers: its sacred buildings, infrastructure, courts and neighbourhoods explain one another.
chapterQuestions: How did one strategic city become a centre of Eastern Roman and Ottoman worlds?
What survives, what was reused and whose community story does each institution tell?
3.geographySummary: Istanbul spans European and Asian shores. Bursa/Cumalıkızık with selected İznik, or Edirne, is an optional second cluster.
3.chronologySummary: Roman and Byzantine imperial city → Ottoman governance and exchange → nineteenth-century reform and representation → modern and contemporary lives.

4.title: Nordic kingdoms
4.hook: A cargo hull, a royal runestone and a workers’ meeting house tell three different histories of the North.

storyBeats.title: The sea carries more than raiders
storyBeats.text: Roskilde's ships distinguish cargo vessels, warships and the craftsmanship behind them. Sea routes connected northern societies with Britain, the Baltic and wider medieval worlds. Jelling's runestones then bring royal claims and Christian conversion into the same monumental landscape.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Tenth-century royal claims; eleventh-century ships

storyBeats.title: Kingdoms make themselves visible
storyBeats.text: Cathedrals, treasuries and the Vasa's carved propaganda place religion, royal hierarchy and naval ambition in material form. The original warship also invites questions about engineering failure and conservation. These objects sit within different Danish, Swedish and Norwegian histories rather than one northern story.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Vasa, 1628; later recovery and conservation

storyBeats.title: Ordinary and Indigenous lives
storyBeats.text: The Workers Museum adds family life, work and labour organisation to the royal sequence; art and design show other modern institutions. Sámi histories take the map beyond national borders. Their languages, livelihoods and rights belong to living societies, not a final museum footnote.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Nineteenth–twenty-first-century labour; living Sámi histories

4.takeaway: Follow movement by sea, then compare the institutions that organised royal power, work and contemporary cultural life.
chapterQuestions: How did maritime societies become Christian kingdoms, Baltic powers and modern societies?
What changes when cargo, labour and Indigenous lives enter a history usually told through rulers?

5.title: Andalusia
5.hook: An Islamic prayer hall, a Christian commission in an Islamic-derived style and an Atlantic archive put successive powers in the same southern cities.

storyBeats.title: Córdoba was a political world
storyBeats.text: The Mosque-Cathedral's columns, mihrab and later crossing expose changing sacred uses. Nearby Medina Azahara adds the infrastructure and ceremonial setting of a caliphal city. The archaeological comparison gives al-Andalus institutions and internal conflict, alongside its celebrated ornament.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Eighth–tenth-century mosque and caliphal Córdoba

storyBeats.title: Conquest changes the patron
storyBeats.text: At Seville's Alcázar, Christian rulers commissioned Islamic-derived artistic forms. Granada's Nasrid palaces stand beside later Christian overlays. These places show influence continuing through changed sovereignty; Jewish buildings and interpretation also demand attention to unequal status, persecution and expulsion.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Medieval Islamic and later Christian palace layers

storyBeats.title: The river opens an Atlantic chapter
storyBeats.text: Seville's port history and Archivo General de Indias move the account from courtly space to imperial administration overseas. Records and exhibitions connect European wealth to conquest and coerced labour. Painting, patios, flamenco and a chosen landscape branch keep the southern cities larger than a medieval religious survey.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Sixteenth–nineteenth-century Atlantic documentation

5.takeaway: Distinguish the origin of an artistic form from the ruler, institution and unequal relationships that commissioned its later use.
chapterQuestions: How did Islamic Iberia, Christian conquest, Jewish life and Atlantic empire reshape the same cities?
Which parts of a palace or sacred building reveal a change of patron and sovereignty?

6.title: Paris and northern France
6.kicker: ROYAL LIGHT, REVOLUTION & THE MODERN CITY
6.hook: Royal stained glass, revolutionary prison rooms and paintings in a railway station let the city’s changing authority become visible.

storyBeats.title: Sacred prestige and court ceremony
storyBeats.text: Sainte-Chapelle's glass once framed a royal collection of eastern Christian relics. Saint-Denis joins kingship to a burial landscape; Versailles later organises court display through rooms and garden axes. Different kinds of royal authority become tangible in light, movement and controlled space.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Thirteenth-century sacred prestige; seventeenth–eighteenth-century court

storyBeats.title: A capital changes its public
storyBeats.text: The Conciergerie turns from royal palace to revolutionary detention and tribunal. Paris's redesigned boulevards and public spaces bring another institutional world into view. At Orsay, works from 1848–1914 share a former railway station, linking artistic experiments with urbanisation, leisure and new ways of seeing.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Revolutionary Tribunal, 1793–1795; art, 1848–1914

storyBeats.title: Normandy has its own sequence
storyBeats.text: Rouen, Caen and Bayeux lead through ducal and cross-Channel histories, religious buildings and later memory. A selected D-Day coast circuit brings terrain and individual lives to the account of 1944. Coastal painting or the tidal bay of Mont-Saint-Michel offers a different regional emphasis.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Medieval Normandy; 1944 and postwar commemoration

6.takeaway: Read changes in political legitimacy through the spaces, images and landscapes that successive publics inherited.
chapterQuestions: How did royal-Christian France become a centre of revolution, modern urban life and artistic reinvention?
How do restoration, museum display and commemoration change the evidence you encounter?

7.title: Florence–Tuscany–Venice
7.hook: A civic square, a cathedral dome, a telescope and a Venetian mosaic show wealth turning into different ways of making and knowing.

storyBeats.title: A city funds its image
storyBeats.text: Florence's cathedral complex ties engineering to collective ambition and artistic competition. Palazzo Vecchio records the movement from communal government toward Medici rule. Uffizi paintings place mythological bodies and new representations of space beside devotional images, all shaped by patrons and institutions.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Medieval and Renaissance Florence

storyBeats.title: Looking becomes a craft
storyBeats.text: Sculpture, painting and instruments belong in the same inquiry. At Museo Galileo, telescopes and measuring devices join mathematical ideas to skilled manufacture and court patronage. Tuscan civic places and cultivated landscapes provide settings beyond the museum room for this exchange of knowledge and resources.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Sixteenth–eighteenth-century instruments

storyBeats.title: Venice has a parallel Renaissance
storyBeats.text: St Mark's gold mosaics and transferred objects connect sacred identity to Byzantine inheritance, commerce and conquest. Painting, printing, trading communities and the lagoon give Venice its own account of artistic life. Comparing it with Florence makes the Renaissance a set of connected urban histories.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Medieval and Renaissance Venice; later interpretation

7.takeaway: Follow who paid for images and knowledge, then compare the civic and maritime worlds in which they were made.
chapterQuestions: How did commercial cities turn wealth, competition and classical learning into art and new ways of knowing?
What differs between a Florentine civic commission and a Venetian sacred or maritime object?

connectedLegs.text: Classical Roman sculpture and architecture become reference material for Renaissance artists; the papacy recruits the same artists trained in Tuscany.
Venice inherits and appropriates Byzantine art and objects and remains entangled with Ottoman commerce and war.
Italian techniques, artists, and court culture spread into France; Paris collections allow comparison with their original settings.
Spanish royal collecting brings Venetian painting into the Prado, connecting Titian and court power across Europe.
Merchant wealth and workshops also shape the northern Renaissance; compare Italian perspective and sculpture with Netherlandish oil painting.
Humanist books, scientific instruments, and later collecting connect the Italian Renaissance to British intellectual and museum history.
Venice’s maritime empire leaves buildings and political relationships along the Adriatic rather than ending at the lagoon.

8.title: Madrid and Castile
8.hook: A royal portrait, an in-situ El Greco and Guernica turn the representation of power into a question rather than a conclusion.

storyBeats.title: Castile has layered foundations
storyBeats.text: Toledo holds Roman, Visigothic, Islamic, Jewish and Christian histories in the same city. Its buildings and collections reveal exchange alongside unequal power and expulsion. Segovia's engineering and fortified urban settings add another view of the territorial world that preceded Madrid's court.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Roman and medieval Iberian layers

storyBeats.title: A monarchy collects Europe
storyBeats.text: The Prado brings Venetian, Netherlandish and Spanish works into a royal collecting history. El Escorial concentrates monarchy, religion and knowledge; Las Descalzas adds royal women and religious communities as patrons. The scale of a court is also visible in the connections of its artists and objects.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Fifteenth–nineteenth-century collecting; sixteenth–seventeenth-century patronage

storyBeats.title: Paintings answer back
storyBeats.text: Velázquez and Goya complicate royal grandeur; El Greco's painting remains in its commissioned Toledo church. At the Reina Sofía, Guernica carries the sequence into civilian suffering and modern political violence. Salamanca adds a university setting for learning and debates over justice and conquest.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Sixteenth-century El Greco; twentieth-century art and older university traditions

8.takeaway: Ask how images legitimise authority, who commissions them and when art opens a space for criticism.
chapterQuestions: How did diverse Iberian societies become a monarchy with global reach?
How do an original church setting, a royal collection and modern political art change your reading of an image?
8.geographySummary: Madrid is the principal base, with Toledo and Segovia as compact city satellites. El Escorial/Guadarrama or the western Ávila–Salamanca branch requires choosing an emphasis.
8.chronologySummary: Roman and medieval Iberian layers → Castilian consolidation → global monarchy and collecting → artistic criticism → civil war and modern memory.

connectedLegs.text: Segovia and Madrid’s archaeological collections continue the Roman provincial story outside Italy.
Toledo’s Islamic and Mudéjar layers and later Castilian expansion must be read alongside al-Andalus, not as an isolated Christian narrative.
El Greco’s Greek and Venetian formation and Titian’s Spanish royal commissions connect Iberian art to Italy and the eastern Mediterranean.
Portuguese and Castilian maritime empires developed in competition and negotiated divisions of overseas claims.
The Habsburg monarchy ruled the Low Countries, collected northern painting, and became entangled in Dutch revolt and independence.
Atlantic rivalry and royal collecting connect Spanish and British histories; Goya also bridges European war and political criticism.
Guernica introduces the violence and artistic responses that recur in the twentieth-century Berlin-Poland chapter.

9.title: Portugal
9.hook: A carved cloister, a rebuilt street grid and a vineyard terrace connect royal ambition to labour, trade and lives across the Atlantic.

storyBeats.title: The waterfront gathers the world
storyBeats.text: Belém's monuments and maritime collections connect a Portuguese kingdom to navigation, religious imagery and long-distance exchange. Jerónimos turns ambition into carved architecture. Works and objects shaped by African and Asian connections widen the frame; the Lagos slavery exhibition makes coercion central to the account.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Fifteenth–sixteenth-century maritime worlds; later interpretation

storyBeats.title: A capital rebuilds
storyBeats.text: The earthquake opens a different Lisbon chapter. Baixa's planned grid and Praça do Comércio show state-led reconstruction after 1755. Older archaeology and the ruins of Carmo keep earlier urban layers in view, so reform becomes legible through what was retained, lost and reorganised.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Reconstruction after 1755

storyBeats.title: Export landscapes and later freedoms
storyBeats.text: Porto's riverfront and the Douro's cultivated slopes belong to one commercial network. Terraces, producers and agricultural labour supply the countryside behind the export city. Fado and modern art add living culture; Aljube follows dictatorship, colonial war, resistance and democratic change.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Centuries of cultivation; twentieth-century resistance and 1974

9.takeaway: Follow a commodity, an object or a ship beyond the monument, including the labour and coercion that made the network possible.
chapterQuestions: How did an Atlantic-facing kingdom connect continents through navigation, commerce, conquest and forced labour?
How do reconstruction, working landscapes and democratic memory extend a maritime account?

9.chronologySummary: Medieval Islamic and Christian layers → maritime expansion and global exchange → earthquake reconstruction → export landscapes → dictatorship, anti-colonial struggles and democracy.

10.title: Belgium–Netherlands
10.hook: A painted panel, a printing press and a canal share a question: how did northern towns organise wealth and circulate ideas?

storyBeats.title: Merchants and sacred pictures
storyBeats.text: Flemish market squares, belfries and religious communities place urban commerce beside civic power. The Ghent Altarpiece joins close observation to Christian symbolism and patronage. Movement, conflict and conservation later became part of its material history.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Medieval towns and the Ghent Altarpiece, 1432

storyBeats.title: Belief changes the market
storyBeats.text: Plantin-Moretus makes the circulation of books and ideas visible through presses, type and a surviving workshop. Religious conflict and Habsburg rule help frame the region's later division. Southern Catholic commissions and Dutch civic and private patrons offer different settings for artists and institutions.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Sixteenth–eighteenth-century print and religious networks

storyBeats.title: The water city reaches overseas
storyBeats.text: Amsterdam's planned canals and merchant houses connect prosperity to organised urban building. Pictures and maritime objects must also be read through colonial violence and slavery. Kinderdijk, modern barriers and Rotterdam's port reveal the continuing collective work behind a landscape often seen only as scenery.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Sixteenth–seventeenth-century urban growth; continuing water management

10.takeaway: Follow how patronage, print, commerce and water management join private wealth to public institutions.
chapterQuestions: How did commerce, religious division, art, science and overseas power transform the Low Countries?
Who produced the wealth pictured in a gallery or built into a merchant street?

10.chronologySummary: Medieval mercantile towns → Burgundian and northern Renaissance patronage → Habsburg rule and religious conflict → Dutch Republic and oceanic trade → modern water systems, art and memory.

11.title: Prague–Vienna–Budapest
11.hook: A Gothic royal church, a court garden and a historicist parliament make one imperial region’s different claims to authority visible.

storyBeats.title: Bohemian kingship and urban communities
storyBeats.text: Prague's castle and St Vitus connect local kingship to Charles IV's imperial city and pan-European craftsmanship. The Hussite challenge adds religious contest to the account. Josefov's synagogues, ritual objects and cemetery stones place centuries of Jewish urban life beside later persecution and memory.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Fourteenth-century Gothic beginning; medieval–modern community histories

storyBeats.title: Vienna stages and questions the court
storyBeats.text: Schönbrunn's rooms and garden axes organise Habsburg ceremony; collections and musical institutions give court culture other forms. Around 1900, Secession artists connected painting, architecture, design and music through new collaborations. Freud's museum adds another kind of intellectual history to the city.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Seventeenth–nineteenth-century court; modernism around 1900

storyBeats.title: Budapest shows another capital
storyBeats.text: Roman Aquincum and an Ottoman bath sit within Hungary's layered account. The Parliament combines nineteenth-century political identity with much older royal regalia. Read these cities through imperial collapse and twentieth-century conflict while preserving their art, neighbourhoods, gardens and living culture.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Roman and Ottoman layers; late nineteenth–early twentieth-century parliament

11.takeaway: Compare imperial authority with local institutions, artistic dissent and the older symbols reused by modern states.
chapterQuestions: How did a diverse imperial region create great cities, art, music and ideas, then fragment into modern states?
Which older forms and symbols were reused to express a newer political identity?

12.title: Alpine Europe
12.hook: A prehistoric coat, a monastery manuscript and a railway viaduct show that the mountains have long been inhabited, organised and crossed.

storyBeats.title: People were already here
storyBeats.text: Ötzi's body, clothing and equipment make Copper Age adaptation tangible. Later towns, monasteries, regional powers and civic communities show inhabited mountains rather than empty scenery. At St Gall, manuscripts and the monastery plan join sacred architecture to the organisation of learning and daily life.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Copper Age adaptation; medieval monastic learning

storyBeats.title: A landscape takes work
storyBeats.text: Lavaux's terraces link monastic organisation, labour and regional economies to cultivated slopes. Village interiors, language and craft keep local societies visible. Glacial landforms and habitats belong to longer environmental histories, with contemporary change forming part of the present encounter.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Eleventh-century cultivation onward; geological and present environmental time

storyBeats.title: Engineering changes the crossing
storyBeats.text: Transport collections and the Albula–Bernina railway connect difficult terrain to viaducts, tunnels and new patterns of mobility. Railways, cableways and tourism altered access and local economies. The journey's views become more meaningful when the technologies and communities supporting them remain in sight.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Nineteenth-century mobility onward; early twentieth-century railway

chapterQuestions: How did Europe live with, cross, interpret and transform its mountain barrier?
What work, knowledge and local institutions sit behind a scenic view?

13.title: Britain
13.kicker: FROM STONE CIRCLES TO INDUSTRIAL SYSTEMS
13.hook: A stone circle, a meridian and an iron bridge connect coordinated ritual, global navigation and the changing organisation of work.

storyBeats.title: Before and beyond Roman Britain
storyBeats.text: Wiltshire's circles, earthworks and burial landscapes put monumental engineering before literate empires. Roman provincial sites, Anglo-Saxon objects and York's Norse evidence then reveal several connected worlds. Britain's story changes when England and Scotland are read as interacting histories rather than one interchangeable setting.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Neolithic–Bronze Age monuments; later Norse settlement

storyBeats.title: Authority and knowledge share a city
storyBeats.text: Westminster joins sacred kingship, parliamentary space and national remembrance. Greenwich's clocks, astronomy and navigation connect measurement to commerce, naval power and imperial administration. Museum collections bring distant material cultures to London, with acquisition and disputed ownership belonging to their histories.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Medieval–present authority; seventeenth–nineteenth-century science and collecting

storyBeats.title: Production changes the landscape
storyBeats.text: Bath and Edinburgh make Georgian urbanism and Enlightenment settings visible. Ironbridge and Manchester show resources, machines, workers and transport organised into new systems. Art, household and port histories make industrial and imperial change an account of communities as well as inventions.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Eighteenth–nineteenth-century industry and urban change

13.takeaway: Connect institutions and technologies to their effects on ordinary lives, landscapes and the objects held in museums.
chapterQuestions: How did an island at the edge of Roman Europe become a centre of parliament, science, industry and global empire?
How did measurement and production alter work, movement and authority?

14.title: Berlin–Poland
14.hook: A royal hill, a border through a street and a shipyard place older cultural lives beside the forces that threatened and transformed them.

storyBeats.title: Begin with the lives that existed
storyBeats.text: Kraków's royal and urban settings, painting collections, craft and Jewish communities establish histories before the twentieth century. Berlin's museums and Wittenberg's Reformation offer other institutional paths. These earlier lives and ideas give later violence a fuller historical frame.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Medieval and early modern lives; later remembrance

storyBeats.title: Power reaches the everyday
storyBeats.text: Nazi institutions and Auschwitz-Birkenau require evidence, individual lives and respectful reflection. In Berlin, the Wall's structures and neighbourhood traces show an international boundary entering homes and daily movement. Jewish museums keep centuries of community life visible alongside persecution and remembrance.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Nazi persecution and genocide; Cold War division

storyBeats.title: Cities rebuild and citizens act
storyBeats.text: Warsaw's reconstructed centre and Dresden's rebuilding make preservation a deliberate public choice. Gdańsk's shipyard and Solidarity interpretation place workers and civil society among the actors of political change. Art, markets and nature give space to absorb memory while keeping the region larger than its catastrophes.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Twentieth-century reconstruction and late-century civic action

14.takeaway: Read the evidence of violence carefully, alongside the long cultural lives, public choices and civic action that it affected.
chapterQuestions: How did diverse societies produce national states, dictatorship, genocide, division, resistance and renewal?
What is original, reconstructed, absent or commemorated in the city you see?
14.geographySummary: Choose Berlin with two further bases: Kraków–Warsaw, Dresden–Kraków, or Gdańsk–Warsaw. Southern-Poland and mountain branches are substitutions.
14.chronologySummary: Royal, religious, Jewish and artistic worlds → Reformation and national public institutions → dictatorship and genocide → divided cities and socialist states → resistance, reconstruction and civic renewal.

15.title: Adriatic–Balkan crossroads
15.hook: People still live within a Roman palace; a rebuilt bridge and a travelled manuscript ask how inherited places and cultures survive change.

storyBeats.title: The palace becomes a city
storyBeats.text: Split's Peristyle, cellars, cathedral and residential streets turn an imperial complex into evidence of continuing adaptation. Trogir adds Venetian networks; Dubrovnik's walls, institutions and harbour belong to a distinct maritime republic. Earthquake, war and rebuilding complicate the appearance of untouched old towns.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Late Roman fabric; medieval maritime cities and later rebuilding

storyBeats.title: A different urban world inland
storyBeats.text: Mostar's bridge, bazaars and domestic heritage connect Ottoman frontier institutions to later layers and reconstruction. Sarajevo's civic spaces and museum branches bring Ottoman, Jewish and Habsburg histories together. The Haggadah traces Iberian Jewish culture, diaspora movement and preservation across European crises.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Ottoman and Habsburg layers; Jewish diaspora and modern preservation

storyBeats.title: Landscapes and later publics
storyBeats.text: Karst, rivers, islands and cultivated plains explain movement and livelihoods across the region. Slovenia offers another Roman and Habsburg setting, with Plečnik's civic designs creating symbolic capital spaces after imperial dissolution. Modern art and civilian memories extend the account while daily culture keeps conflict from defining the whole chapter.
storyBeats.timeLabel: Interwar civic design; contemporary civilian memory

15.takeaway: Compare adaptation and reconstruction in inhabited places, following the communities and objects that crossed political borders.
chapterQuestions: What happens where Roman, Christian, Venetian, Habsburg, Ottoman, Jewish and Yugoslav worlds overlap?
How can a reused building, a rebuilt bridge and a migrated manuscript tell different kinds of continuity?
15.geographySummary: Choose Dalmatia–Bosnia or Slovenia–north Croatia. A southern core links Split, Mostar and Sarajevo, with Dubrovnik selected only when pace permits.
15.chronologySummary: Roman and early Christian layers → medieval maritime cities and Venetian connections → Ottoman and Habsburg urban worlds → imperial dissolution, Yugoslavia and later war → reconstruction and living culture.
